Wildfire forces evacuation of 1,000 as flames sweep Croatia’s coast Copy/paste the link below: Copy Copy/paste the article video embed link below: Copy Updated: 14/08/2026 - 9:41 GMT+2 Croatia is battling a wildfire that swept through vegetation and homes in Lokva Rogoznica on Thursday, 13 August, forcing about 1,000 residents and tourists to evacuate. … More More than 150 firefighters were deployed as strong winds pushed flames through pine forests and towards residential areas on the Adriatic coast. Some homes and vehicles were damaged, while the main coastal road through the town was closed. Most evacuees were taken to nearby Omis, where a sports hall was used as a temporary shelter. Local authorities also reported that some people suffered burns. ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT The blaze came as Croatia faced a prolonged summer heatwave, with high temperatures raising the risk of further fires along the Adriatic. Fire chief Slavko Tucakovic warned that crews faced a difficult night and called in reinforcements from other parts of the country. Four Canadair water-bombing aircraft were placed on standby for the morning because they cannot operate at night. Strong winds were blamed for the rapid spread of the fire, according to Omis deputy mayor Ivan Pivcevic. Another major wildfire on the nearby island of Brac had been brought under control earlier on Thursday. https://www.upi.com/Top_News/World-News/.text: Judge to decide on Tate brothers' extradition over rape charges Aug. 27 (UPI) -- Andrew and Tristan Tate are in federal court in Miami on Thursday for a hearing over their potential extradition to Britain where they face charges of rape and human trafficking. Magistrate Judge Lauren F. Louis is presiding over Thursday's hearing as the Tate brothers have requested their release from detention. The brothers were arrested on July 18. The brothers face 59 criminal charges, including rape, human trafficking and sexual exploitation. They are also charged with human trafficking in Romania in a case that remains open. They have denied the allegations against them. "We are, of course, objecting to extradition because Andrew and Tristan are innocent," Joe McBride, attorney for the Tates, said after their initial hearing on July 20. The U.S. State Department says that, under current U.S. law, it is "extremely rare that an extradition judge will release on bail a person sought in international extradition." After the charges were filed against the Tate brothers, the Trump administration lifted travel restrictions on them, allowing them to fly from Romania to the United States in February 2025, the New York Times reported. On July 23, former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said the White House will not intervene in the case. The United States and Britain signed an extradition treaty in 2003, a pact that defines what constitutes an extraditable offense. Under this definition, a criminal charge that would normally be punished by at least one year in prison in the United States and Britain would meet the criteria for extradition. The British government has until Sept. 16 to file an extradition request to the United States to take the Tates into custody. Prosecutors have described the Tates as a danger to the community and highlighted the risk that they would flee and evade arrest, citing Andrew Tate stating "online that he has seven different passports and 15 driver's licenses." Tate said this in reference to his ability to "prevent authorities from determining his true identity." Andrew Tate is a central figure in the so-called "manosphere," a niche in the social media and podcasting arena known for promoting blatant misogyny with an emphasis on a right-wing version of masculinity. If the judge rules against them on Thursday, the Tates may request judicial review and could appeal. Such an appeal could elevate to the U.S. Supreme Court . McBride named Justice Clarence Thomas specifically while discussing the idea of seeking relief from the high court. While the current charges against the Tates center on Europe, they have also been the subjects of an investigation in Florida. Andrew Tate was named in a subpoena by a grand jury in New York in 2023. Published: 9:43 AM, Sep 20, 2026 Russian President Vladimir Putin delivers a speech during a ceremony SHARE WASHINGTON: The Russia sanctions bill signed into law by US President Donald Trump on Friday gives him new ​powers to impose tariffs that could last well beyond his presidency, injecting more ​uncertainty into the global economy after nearly two years of trade wars. The immediate impact may be limited, given Trump's reluctance to take actions that could push consumer prices higher ahead of the November midterm elections, when control of Congress is at stake, analysts said. But critics say the legislation, which imposes tariffs on Russia's biggest trading partners, has broad language that could herald trouble for other countries as well if they find themselves in Trump's crosshairs in the future. The bill requires Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100% within 30 days on all goods imported into the US from the five largest importers of Russian crude oil or gas as well as any country that knowingly made new purchases of oil or gas 30 days after the law was enacted or was among the top five countries helping Russia evade ⁠sanctions. China and India are among the biggest buyers of Russian oil, but critics say the law gives US officials enough leeway to name a range of targets since it does not name any country ⁠or spell out how the top-five lists would be calculated. "Given the discretionary authority that the president has, it is likely to be abused," said Laura Brank, a lawyer at Bryan Cave Leighton Paisner who focuses on cross-border transactions. Since returning to office in January 2025, Trump has imposed tariffs of up to 50% on more than 80 countries, though the Supreme Court has struck down many of them, saying he exceeded his authority. Trump has cited a variety of reasons, including disagreements with foreign leaders, for his actions. Challenging the latest tariffs ‌in court could be difficult since the law specifically calls for the duties, while previous challenges to tariffs have successfully ​argued that the Trump administration misapplied laws from decades earlier. US ⁠Representative Don Beyer, a Virginia Democrat, argued that Trump had wrongly used existing trade laws to pursue his agenda in the past and is likely to do the same ​with the new law. The White House has denied abusing any trade ‌laws. "We don’t know when, but you don’t need a crystal ball to know what is likely to happen next," Beyer said on social media. Once Trump agreed to move forward with the bill in July after over a year of delays, US officials pushed for quick passage to give Trump additional leverage in his meeting with Chinese President Xi ​Jinping next week, according to congressional sources. US officials have tried to reassure lawmakers that the measure has sufficient guardrails, while acknowledging its significance in handing control of tariffs to the White House. "It is the first time in nearly forty years that Congress has granted new tariff authorities to the executive branch," White House legislative director James Braid said in a post on X on Wednesday. The White House did not respond to a request for comment on concerns about the broader scope of the measure. LACK OF CLARITY ON TARGET COUNTRIES The sweeping package, which passed Congress on Wednesday, aims to deprive Russia of funds used to pay for its nearly five-year war on Ukraine. The legislation authorizes sanctions against Russia's energy and defense industries, as well as ‌its "shadow fleet" of tankers used to evade existing sanctions. Moscow on Thursday said further US sanctions against Russia would make it harder to reach a peace deal in Ukraine. Jeannette Chu, vice president of the National Foreign ​Trade Council, a trade group that advocates for open trade, said different entities had differing assessments of which countries could be hit with tariffs since no firm criteria were spelled out. The countries speculated as likely include Brazil, ​India, Japan and countries in ‌the European ⁠Union, she said. China said it "consistently opposed long-arm jurisdiction that lacks a basis in international law" while India warned Washington that new tariffs could impact bilateral ties. In a worst-case scenario, Chu said, Ukraine itself could suffer if the new tariffs cut off Russian oil and gas supplies for refined products in EU countries, given it relies on diesel from refineries in Hungary and Slovakia. Not everyone agrees the bill gives the Trump administration too much leeway. The conservative think ​tank Foundation for Defense of Democracies argues that the bill lays out sufficient criteria on which countries can be hit and rejects the idea that it gives ⁠Trump a back door to ​imposing other tariffs. It noted that the original version of the bill required even higher tariffs of 500%. RISKY TIMING Any new duties would have to be announced just days before the midterm elections, which could push oil prices higher at a time when voters are already unhappy over rising costs. Trump's popularity has declined since he launched a war on Iran in February that has disrupted oil shipments from the Middle East. "Given the state of the current energy markets, it certainly seems risky," said Ryan Majerus, a former senior US official who served under both Democratic and Republican presidents and is now with law firm King & Spalding. He says Trump could get around the timing issue by imposing a ​zero-rate tariff and revising it later, at will. Others say Trump's reluctance to take tough action against Russia since returning to office raises questions about how he will implement the legislation, which also gives ​Trump broad authority to waive tariffs or sanctions for national security reasons. That would let him avoid hitting Moscow or its backers harder, simply by notifying Congress, they said. "This is entirely discretionary," said Ben Harris, a former senior Treasury Department official under former Democratic President Joe Biden. "The definitions are vague and the president has kind of a get-out-of-jail-free card in the form of a waiver." Oman Observer is now on the WhatsApp channel. https://www.politico.eu/article/andy-bur.text: Prime Minister Andy Burnham will have an unofficial goal when he meets members of Britain’s former empire next week: Avoid a fight about slavery reparations. Good luck, as they say, with that. His predecessor Keir Starmer’s trip to the last Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting, at a beach resort on the Pacific island of Samoa in 2024, is still the stuff of rueful mutters in parts of Whitehall. Advertisement Lined up in a semi-circle of armchairs — “like an Alcoholics Anonymous meeting,” as one person briefed on the gathering put it — leaders from many of the 56 Commonwealth nations negotiated live over a 16-page communique on laptops and tablets. Starmer, a barrister, found himself personally redrafting a key paragraph about reparations on a screen surrounded by other leaders, said two further people briefed on the meeting. The unusually intimate format of the leaders’ retreat meant they had no officials with them on the veranda, and Starmer had just one civil servant — No. 10’s private secretary for foreign affairs — stationed in a tent close by. His chief of staff Morgan McSweeney was woken at 4 a.m. London time by a phone call to talk about the strategy for reparations. That, however, was never clearly resolved. The retreat dragged on hours late; some leaders left before it was even over. Starmer was frustrated and felt he had been “ambushed,” said one U.K. official involved in the 2024 trip. A second said they had blocked the incident from their memory. A third said Starmer was left “furious,” adding: “He went in blind and it was terrible for him.” A fourth said simply: “It was a disaster.” All were granted anonymity to speak frankly. The eventual communique agreed on a “conversation towards forging a common future based on equity.” This fudge kicked the issue of reparations down the road — where it now lands in Burnham’s lap. Britain’s new prime minister will touch down at the biennial summit in Antigua and Barbuda next week to find the issue still firmly on some Caribbean and African leaders’ minds. At the United Nations in May, 123 countries passed a motion calling for “inclusive, good-faith dialogue on reparatory justice.” The U.K. abstained. Barbados PM Mia Mottley announced a manifesto from Caribbean leaders on the “moral, ethical and legal case” for reparations in June. Commonwealth Secretary-General Shirley Botchwey said last week that an apology for Britain’s role in the slave trade “wouldn’t hurt.” Advertisement The visit will be a test of how Burnham — who has a reputation for speaking off the cuff, especially on issues of moral justice — maintains a delicate U.K. government line that reparations are not “the answer,” as Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband told POLITICO last month . And Burnham will face that challenge in a unique spotlight: It will be his first overseas visit with King Charles III, who is the head of the Commonwealth. POLITICO spoke to a dozen U.K. officials or politicians who were involved in the 2024 summit or the planning for Burnham’s upcoming visit. They painted a picture of acute anxiety in the British state over how to deal with calls for reparations from its former colonies; tensions between Downing Street and the Foreign Office over the handling of 2024; and serious questions in Whitehall about whether the summit is even useful for No. 10 — despite the king’s role leaving U.K. prime ministers little choice but to attend. Burnham will not have to deal with the extreme jetlag and communications hurdles that dogged Starmer’s trip, which involved a 28-hour flight in each direction. But like Starmer, he will fly out at a time when his in-tray is crowded by other issues — not least the U.S. midterms happening at the same time and the domestic aftermath of his first budget, just unveiled this past Wednesday. Keir Starmer attends a a state banquet during the CHOGM summit in Samoa, on Oct. 24, 2024. | Pool photo by Fiona Goodall via Getty Images The first U.K. official quoted earlier in this story said: “There’s a sense that there can’t be a repeat of [2024] this time around.” The third U.K. official quoted above said: “I don’t understand why they’re making the same mistake. Does the prime minister really have to go?” A No. 10 official, however, said Burnham made clear soon after taking power on July 20 that he was “very keen” to attend the summit. Miliband has “laid the groundwork so that things hopefully won’t be as tricky as they were in 2024,” this person added. “Andy’s style is that he is an honest broker with people, and he will give an instinctive response to things,” the official said. “But the government’s position is clear that reparations are not seen as the right route. It’s a careful balancing act, but one that we’re well prepared for.” Advertisement Climate resilience fund in the works One tactic for the current No. 10 will be to try to avoid talking about it public. Downing Street has broken with recent precedent by deciding not to bring the usual “pack” of political journalists, taking a smaller media “pool” instead. This will limit the scope of questions that Burnham faces. (Political editors from news outlets, including POLITICO, have written to No. 10 to object to the arrangement.) Timing could also allow the visit to slip under the radar. Burnham and Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband will be there alongside counterparts including Anthony Albanese of Australia and Mark Carney of Canada, creating a rare opportunity for them to discuss the implications of the U.S. midterm results in private. The symbolism, as “middle power” nations deal with a drift in U.S. relations under Donald Trump, would be obvious. British PM Andy Burnham, center, leaves the stage at the end of the Labour Conference in Liverpool on Sept. 30, 2026. | Ian Forsyth/Getty Images Officially, the agenda is to build an alliance that can boost these middle powers, along with the developing states that global summits usually overlook. The Commonwealth Secretariat — the London-based body that co-ordinates the summit — said the aim of next week’s gathering is “partnerships and investment,” including in climate and youth employment, and removing trade barriers. Likewise, the U.K. Foreign Office has been working on a climate resilience fund for developing nations, two people with knowledge of the talks said. A third said conversations in the U.K. government had focused on mobilizing public and private finance, and improving access to finance for climate-vulnerable countries. Advertisement Three people with knowledge of the planning emphasized that this summit would be an opportunity to build on relations with countries that could discuss bilateral trade, though they did not name specific nations and no U.K. trade ministers are due at the event. “There will obviously be trade and investment discussions with a range of partners,” said one of the three people, a U.K. government official, who also noted that the U.K. will raise the impacts of El Niño. “The bigger picture is that we want to use the Commonwealth network to deepen trade and investment links across its 56 members — that Commonwealth advantage is one of the reasons the grouping matters to the UK.” ‘Playing Scrabble with words’ But leaders at these events, known by the awkward acronym CHOGM, can raise whatever topics they wish — reparations included. Denis O’Brien, the Irish telecoms billionaire who founded the Repair Campaign calling for financial reparations to the Caribbean in 2022, said: “The conversation has moved radically forward.” He urged Britain and other European nations to “start off with an apology and then have an engagement,” adding: “The Foreign Office and the prime minister’s office are playing Scrabble with words — and unfortunately they’re leaving King Charles, who is so highly respected in the Caribbean, in a very difficult position.” Paul Boateng, the Labour peer who was Britain’s first Black Cabinet minister and now campaigns on the issue, said Caribbean nations “are going to be pressing it. This issue is not going to go away.” The recent UN resolution reinforced Caribbean and African nations’ argument, argued Boateng: “We can’t be seen to simply ignore it … We cannot hold the Foreign Office line that it changes nothing.” That position cast a long shadow two years ago. Advertisement No. 10 flew to Samoa in 2024 insisting reparations were “not on the agenda,” even though the summit’s free-wheeling format meant the choice was effectively out of Downing Street’s hands. This message “went down like a bag of sick” with Caribbean nations who saw it as “colonial” and “arrogant,” recalled one person involved in conversations at the time. The handling created tension between Downing Street and the Foreign Office, then led by David Lammy, who also attended, according to six other people with knowledge of the 2024 trip. King Charles and Queen Camilla attend the bestowing and farewell ceremony on Oct. 26, 2024. | Pool photo by Manaui Faulalo via Getty Images One of the six people said No. 10 figures had expected the Foreign Office to better manage expectations among Commonwealth nations ahead of Starmer’s arrival. The person said: “No. 10 did not feel like they were well enough informed, and felt some of this could and should have been handled in advance. There was the feeling that both Lammy and the Foreign Office were institutionally pre-disposed to this sort of stuff and not shutting it down. The PM didn’t know what he was going into.” A second person said: “​​The FCDO world does forget, sometimes, the politics of what’s going on in the U.K. It’s very institutionalized.” A third person stressed that senior aides in No. 10 had blamed Foreign Office officials, not Lammy personally. Before Starmer left office this year, No. 10 had been drawing up plans for Starmer to skip this year’s CHOGM — and send Lammy as his representative. By then Lammy had been moved from the foreign office and was Starmer’s deputy prime minister. Advertisement Another of the six people countered that it was No. 10 that persisted, ahead of the 2024 summit, with a line that was too binary — reparatory justice, as campaigners prefer to call it, has a wide definition that includes support for climate adaptation and education — and failed to listen to Foreign Office warnings ahead of time about the strength of feeling among Commonwealth nations. “The audit trail would completely exonerate David and the Foreign Office,” this person said. They argued No. 10 officials — who were keen to hold on to the mantle of fiscal responsibility ahead of Starmer’s first budget — had viewed the row too much through how it would be perceived by the right-wing Daily Mail newspaper. Two other people with knowledge of the 2024 trip insisted they did not remember any significant friction between No. 10 and the Foreign Office. Lammy’s office did not immediately respond to an invitation to comment. UK review mooted a scaled-back summit More significantly, the 2024 summit also led to discussions in Whitehall about the set-up of CHOGM itself. Lammy commissioned an internal review by Foreign Office officials on the Commonwealth in the wake of the 2024 summit, his former Special Adviser Ben Judah told POLITICO. Judah said the review suggested reducing the frequency of CHOGMs to “every four or five years,” potentially aligned with the hosting of the Commonwealth Games, and seeking to remove the final communique and leaders’ retreat. Advertisement It suggested an investment conference in alternate years modeled on the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum, which could keep the Commonwealth branding but with no organizational role for the Secretariat, said Judah. Judah suggested this would improve attendance at CHOGM, which is often patchy; India’s Prime Minister Narendra Modi does not plan to attend next week’s summit, for example, though there will be a delegation led by External Affairs Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar. “The Indians think this thing is ridiculous and self-harming and just totally bizarre,” said Judah. “They’d be interested in a real investment conference, not this farce.” A second former U.K. government official said they knew about the report, which has not been made public, adding that No. 10 figures under Starmer discussed similar concerns about the format of the Commonwealth summit after the Samoa visit. Starmer sits with other leaders during the opening ceremony of CHOGM 2024 in Apia, Samoa. | Fiona Goodall/Getty Images The Foreign Office declined to respond to questions about the report when contacted by POLITICO, including when it was finalized or whether any of its recommendations were pursued. One Foreign Office official, however, stressed that it was not the U.K. government’s position and that any decisions about future CHOGM arrangements would be for Commonwealth members collectively. The U.K. government official quoted on trade and investment earlier in this piece said: “The Commonwealth is more important to our geostrategic position now than at any time throughout its 80-year history. In today’s more divided, unpredictable world, the Commonwealth has the potential to be a powerful, values-based force for good in the world. “This gives us a huge opportunity to drive U.K. interests and priorities — Commonwealth relationships have helped to drive global support for Ukraine, and it is hugely important for our work on climate.” Advertisement Funding pulled from reserves Judah, however, argued that the Commonwealth Secretariat is a “broken institution” and Britain should wind down its involvement to focus on an investment summit instead. CHOGM has ended up as a “platform for the reparations campaign,” argued Judah: “There’s nothing else on the agenda because it’s not a real international organization, and it’s not a real summit with deliverables.” The Commonwealth and Secretariat, he said, has “essentially been taken over by the only countries that are still really invested in them, which are the Caribbean countries supported by a few African countries, to push the reparations agenda.” For some, that extends to questions about the way the Secretariat spends its money. Two people with knowledge of the situation said part of this year’s CHOGM summit is being paid for out of the Secretariat’s reserves. “There is a real sense of concern about the malaise and drift of the organization,” argued one of the two people. “Financially it’s in a dire, dire state.” A Commonwealth spokesperson responded: “The Commonwealth Secretariat accesses reserve funds for the biennial Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting and always with member country approval.” Back in 2024, Starmer’s most senior aides privately raised the question about whether he should attend the Samoa summit at all. “We were overruled,” said another person who worked under him. Advertisement Whitehall officials initially assumed that Burnham would not go either, until he said otherwise. “To a lot of the Caribbean countries, the word [from officials] was that he wasn’t going to show,” said O’Brien. “I think people were taken aback by that.” But despite Starmer’s experience in 2024, Burnham will attend. Among all other reasons, there is one very obvious one. “It’s very difficult for a prime minister not to go because the king goes,” said one person who worked under Starmer. “It’s important to him.” Burnham’s ‘surer touch’ Once Burnham is in the room, campaigners hope he will at least be a listening ear. Outside the prime minister’s Manchester office No. 10 North is a statue of Abraham Lincoln, commemorating the mill workers who refused to touch raw cotton picked by slaves. Burnham referred to it in his first speech to the United Nations last month. “In 1862, people with little power used it to help those with none on the other side of the world,” he said. “The best change is change like that, bottom-up change led by people.” Advertisement The new prime minister “understands the importance of Manchester as t
